message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consider contacting a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit. | Keep a written receipt when you pay the deposit. Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions before you move out. | | **Notice Requirements** | • 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases.
• 60‑day notice if the lease term is longer than 12 months. | Get the notice in writing and keep a copy. If you receive a notice that seems shorter than required, you may contest it. | | **Habitability** | Landlords must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control, structural integrity, etc. | Document problems (photos, emails). Give the landlord written notice and allow reasonable time to fix issues. | | **Rent Payment** | Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed but cannot exceed 10% of the monthly rent. | Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Entry Rights** | Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, or source of income. | Report any discriminatory actions to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or your local fair‑housing agency. | | **Eviction Process** | Evictions require a court order. The landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit). You have the right to defend yourself in court. | Respond promptly to notices. If you believe the notice is invalid, consult an attorney or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Lease Termination** | Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with proper notice. For fixed‑term leases, you may break the lease only under certain circumstances (e.g., landlord fails to maintain habitability). | Review your lease for any “break‑lease” clauses. Some landlords offer a “lease‑termination fee” or a “subletting” option. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | Landlords may prohibit subletting, but they must do so in writing. If the lease allows it, you can sublet with the landlord’s consent. | Get written permission before subletting. Keep copies of all agreements. | | **Utilities** | The lease should specify which utilities you are responsible for. If the lease is silent, the landlord typically pays for essential services (heat, water, electricity). | Clarify responsibilities early. Keep receipts for any utility payments you make. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office – Consumer Protection Division
• Texas Legal Services Center
• Local tenant‑rights nonprofits (e.g., Texas Tenants Union) | Contact these organizations for free or low‑cost legal assistance. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on deposits, maintenance, entry, subletting, and termination. 2. **Ask for a written itemized list** of any move‑in inspection findings. 3. **Confirm the security deposit limit** and the procedure for its return. 4. **Verify the notice period** required for ending the tenancy. 5. **Check for any “no‑sublet” clause** and whether it’s enforceable. --- #### Need a Sample Lease or Other Contract? If you’d like a template for a residential lease or another type of contract (e.g., a sublease agreement), let me know the details and I can generate a draft for you.

But we might also offer to generate a contract. The user didn't ask for a contract. So we just answer. No tool needed.
